walkthroughs.body_html:
Rate Equations — a core area of A-Level Chemistry.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Rate Equations brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Rate Equations.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: Doubling [A] doubles the rate; doubling [B] has no effect. The rate equation is:
options: rate = k[A]
rate = k[A][B]
rate = k[A]²
rate = k[B]

mcqs.q: The units of k for a reaction that is second order overall (rate in mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹) are:
options: mol⁻¹ dm³ s⁻¹
s⁻¹
mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹
mol⁻² dm⁶ s⁻¹

mcqs.q: Which change increases the value of the rate constant k?
options: Raising the temperature
Increasing the concentration of a reactant
Grinding a solid reactant more finely
Increasing the volume of the container

mcqs.q: A reaction is zero order with respect to B. Doubling [B]:
options: Leaves the rate unchanged
Doubles the rate
Quadruples the rate
Halves the rate

mcqs.q: Can the orders in a rate equation be read from the coefficients of the balanced equation?
options: k decreases when more reactant is added because the reactant gets used up.
The overall order always equals the number of products formed.
The order with respect to each reactant equals its coefficient in the balanced equation.
No — orders come only from experimental data; the stoichiometric coefficients tell you nothing about the rate equation.

mcqs.q: Does increasing a reactant's concentration change the rate constant k?
options: Increasing concentration increases k because the reaction goes faster.
No — k depends only on temperature (and the presence of a catalyst); changing concentration changes the rate, not k.
k decreases when more reactant is added because the reactant gets used up.
Zero order means doubling that reactant doubles the rate.

mcqs.q: If a reactant has order zero, does it still take part in the reaction?
options: Yes, it can — zero order means it is consumed in a step after the rate-determining step, so its concentration does not affect the rate.
A zero-order reactant is not actually used up in the reaction.
The overall order always equals the number of products formed.
Zero order means doubling that reactant doubles the rate.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Rate constant k”?
options: The proportionality constant in the rate equation; it increases with temperature and its units depend on the overall order.
The slowest step in a mechanism; only species involved up to and including this step appear in the rate equation.
k = Ae^(−Ea/RT) shows the rate constant growing with temperature and shrinking with larger activation energy.
An experimentally determined expression, rate = k[A]ᵐ[B]ⁿ, linking the rate to reactant concentrations raised to their orders.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Rate-determining step”?
options: The proportionality constant in the rate equation; it increases with temperature and its units depend on the overall order.
An experimentally determined expression, rate = k[A]ᵐ[B]ⁿ, linking the rate to reactant concentrations raised to their orders.
The slowest step in a mechanism; only species involved up to and including this step appear in the rate equation.
The power to which a concentration is raised in the rate equation; orders must be found by experiment, not from the balanced equation.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Rate equation”?
options: An experimentally determined expression, rate = k[A]ᵐ[B]ⁿ, linking the rate to reactant concentrations raised to their orders.
Comparing initial rates of experiments with different starting concentrations to deduce the order with respect to each reactant.
k = Ae^(−Ea/RT) shows the rate constant growing with temperature and shrinking with larger activation energy.
The power to which a concentration is raised in the rate equation; orders must be found by experiment, not from the balanced equation.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Arrhenius equation”?
options: k = Ae^(−Ea/RT) shows the rate constant growing with temperature and shrinking with larger activation energy.
An experimentally determined expression, rate = k[A]ᵐ[B]ⁿ, linking the rate to reactant concentrations raised to their orders.
The power to which a concentration is raised in the rate equation; orders must be found by experiment, not from the balanced equation.
The slowest step in a mechanism; only species involved up to and including this step appear in the rate equation.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Initial rates method”?
options: The proportionality constant in the rate equation; it increases with temperature and its units depend on the overall order.
An experimentally determined expression, rate = k[A]ᵐ[B]ⁿ, linking the rate to reactant concentrations raised to their orders.
The slowest step in a mechanism; only species involved up to and including this step appear in the rate equation.
Comparing initial rates of experiments with different starting concentrations to deduce the order with respect to each reactant.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Order of reaction”?
options: The proportionality constant in the rate equation; it increases with temperature and its units depend on the overall order.
Comparing initial rates of experiments with different starting concentrations to deduce the order with respect to each reactant.
The power to which a concentration is raised in the rate equation; orders must be found by experiment, not from the balanced equation.
k = Ae^(−Ea/RT) shows the rate constant growing with temperature and shrinking with larger activation energy.
